D. CENTRAL BANK TAPE

Summary — Policy reaction function

The ECB moved into **active measured tightening** during the window. The 10 September hike was unanimous and high-conviction, with Lagarde explicitly rejecting an “insurance” characterization, while the staff projections embedded above-target inflation deeper into the horizon and upgraded growth. The immediate post-hike tape then constrained extrapolation: Vujčić argued that market pricing was being driven mainly by energy, stressed that high energy also weakens demand, and endorsed the observed projection-round pace “for the time being.” The wage data reinforced that brake. The reaction function is therefore **hawkish in direction but controlled in speed: further tightening is projection-gated and increasingly requires evidence that the energy shock is becoming persistent domestic inflation.**

ECB decision + September staff projections — 10 Sep 2026
Importance: ****

Key policy signal:
All three policy rates were raised 25bp, taking the deposit rate to 2.50%, MRO to 2.65% and marginal lending rate to 2.90%. Staff kept 2026 headline inflation at 3.0% but raised 2027 to 2.5% and 2028 to 2.1%; core was projected at 2.5%, 2.6% and 2.3%. Growth was also revised up to 0.9% / 1.4% / 1.5% for 2026–28.

Representative quote:
“robust across a range of scenarios”

Incremental reaction function:
The projections, more than the fully priced hike itself, strengthened the internal case for at least one further move: the staff baseline now assumes persistent core inflation despite resilient growth. The bar for stopping therefore shifted from current headline inflation toward whether incoming data falsify that medium-term pass-through path.

Lagarde — post-meeting press conference — 10 Sep 2026
Importance: ****

Key policy signal:
Lagarde described the hike as a “no brainer,” emphasized unanimity, explicitly said it was not an insurance decision, downplayed neutral-rate estimates as a policy benchmark in the current shock, and declined to rule out further increases.

Representative quote:
“no brainer”

Incremental reaction function:
This raises the conviction attached to the delivered hike and keeps the directional bias upward. It also means the September move should not be treated as a low-conviction hedge that can be mechanically reversed if headline energy softens.

Lagarde — Ouest-France interview — 12 Sep 2026
Importance: ***

Key policy signal:
Lagarde said the inflation shock would probably last longer than expected and broadened the supply narrative beyond the Middle East to include destroyed Russian refining capacity. With activity resilient, she argued that the ECB was obliged to react.

Representative quote:
“will probably last longer than we had expected”

Incremental reaction function:
The energy-risk horizon becomes less dependent on a single geopolitical de-escalation channel. Crude, gas and refined-product conditions all matter for the December projection round and for assessing whether the shock is fading or becoming persistent.

ECB wage tracker + Eurostat labour costs — 16 Sep 2026
Importance: ***

Key policy signal:
Q2 labour-cost growth eased to 3.1% from 3.3%, while the ECB wage tracker pointed to 2.7% in H1 2027, still below the roughly 3% pace described in the tape as consistent with target.

Representative quote:
“modest uptick”

Incremental reaction function:
The wage complex does not yet validate a broad second-round spiral. This is the principal domestic-inflation brake on the terminal rate and creates a direct tension with the staff projection of 2.6% core inflation in 2027.

Vujčić — Reuters interview conducted 16 Sep, published 18 Sep 2026
Importance: ****

Key policy signal:
Vujčić pushed back on oil-led hike extrapolation, arguing that rate-path pricing was “driven mainly by rising energy prices” while the ECB watches a much broader data set. He emphasized that high energy also damages household incomes and growth, and said the June/September quarterly-with-projections pace was “worth maintaining for the time being.”

Representative quote:
“worth maintaining for the time being”

Incremental reaction function:
This is the clearest speed-limit signal in the window. It reduces the case for mechanically extending the hiking sequence into the October non-projection meeting and shifts the next meaningful decision toward a later projection round, conditional on energy, core inflation, wages and growth. The tape itself flags that this pace interpretation rests heavily on one interview and still requires confirmation from other Governing Council voices.

Bottom line — central bank tape

**Direction up, speed controlled.** The hawks won the meeting and the projection baseline; the centre then resisted market extrapolation into a rapid sequence. The durable policy question is whether realised domestic inflation catches up with the staff pass-through model. If core/services and wages remain contained, the projected 2027 inflation path becomes the key falsifiable object; if they re-accelerate, the September move becomes the first leg of a genuine quarterly tightening sequence. Lane’s 15 September interview remains an explicit gap in the supplied tape and should not be inferred.

E. SIGNAL TENSION CHECK

Main contradiction:
The ECB’s September projections embed **persistent future core inflation**—2.6% in 2027—while realised core/services inflation and the wage complex are currently moving in the opposite direction.

Why it matters:
This decides whether the 10 September hike is the first leg of a projection-round tightening sequence or a high-conviction move that nevertheless proves close to terminal.

Implication:
The decisive test is no longer another high energy headline; it is whether realised core/services, wages and the December projection round validate the staff pass-through model before the centre’s speed limit becomes the dominant reaction function.

F. 5 KEY RELEASES TO DIG INTO

**** EUROPEAN CENTRAL BANK — Monetary Policy Decision (10 Sep)
Why it matters: The defining regime event. The ECB converted its conditional tightening option into a unanimous, high-conviction 25bp hike, while the accompanying projections raised medium-term inflation and growth. The later central-bank tape shows that the next question is not direction alone but pace: whether the staff pass-through path survives incoming data strongly enough to justify another projection-round move.

**** EURO ZONE — HICP Final / Core HICP Final (17 Sep)
Why it matters: The decisive post-hike cross-check. Headline ended at 3.2%, but core fell to 2.4% and services to 3.0% while energy reached 14.3%, confirming the shock without yet confirming generalized second-round inflation.

**** EURO ZONE — GDP Revised + Employment (7 Sep)
Why it matters: GDP +0.6% q/q versus +0.4% expected materially strengthened the H2 starting point and reduced the near-term growth cost of ECB tightening, while modest labor-input growth improved the arithmetic quality of the expansion.

*** GERMANY — Producer Prices (18 Sep)
Why it matters: PPI +1.1% m/m and +4.6% y/y showed that the energy shock had moved decisively into the production chain. This is the clearest bridge between the current external shock and the ECB’s feared downstream persistence scenario.

*** GERMANY — Industrial Production (7 Sep)
Why it matters: The -1.1% m/m miss challenged the manufacturing-recovery story. Auto shutdowns distorted the headline, but -2.2% output excluding energy and construction showed that current weakness was broader than one sector.

G. RED TEAM QUESTIONS

1. Is Vujčić’s projection-round “speed limit” genuinely the Governing Council centre, or would post-hike pushback from Schnabel/Nagel/other hawks reopen October or a faster sequence?
2. If realised core remains near 2.4% and the wage tracker near 2.7%, can the December staff round credibly preserve the 2.6% 2027 core projection that currently carries the hawkish case?
3. What observable combination of core/services, wages and inflation expectations would convert the current energy response into a genuine domestic-inflation tightening cycle?
4. How much of Germany’s PPI acceleration will be absorbed in margins under weak industrial demand, and what evidence would show meaningful pass-through into final prices?
5. How much of Q2 GDP’s +0.6% q/q upside came from durable domestic demand versus inventories, net trade or government/fiscal effects?
6. Does Lagarde’s addition of refining-capacity damage mean that energy-risk falsification now requires both crude/gas relief and normalization in refined-product spreads rather than a single geopolitical de-escalation?
7. For EUR, does relative-rate support dominate the adverse terms-of-trade and real-income channel created by the same energy shock?

H. CURRENCY MARKET-CONSENSUS SCAN

### Bottom line

The public institutional EUR/USD view at the start of the window was **not a clean bullish-euro consensus**. ING entered 7 September at spot 1.1623 with a bearish one-month bias, targets of 1.15/1.16/1.18/1.19 across 1M/3M/6M/12M, and a year-end target cut to 1.16 from 1.18 because a September Fed hike was expected to keep short US rates elevated. MUFG’s September outlook was more constructive beyond Q3, with 1.15 for Q3 and 1.18 for Q4, while its displayed consensus line was 1.16 for both Q3 and Q4. BNP Paribas Wealth Management retained a structurally bearish-dollar view, with 1.16 at three months and 1.20 at twelve months.

Source anchors: ING, 7 Sep 2026; MUFG, September 2026 Monthly Foreign Exchange Outlook; BNP Paribas Wealth Management, Currencies Focus — September 2026.

The centre of gravity shifted more dollar-supportive during the window. After the Fed’s 16 September hike and hawkish signal, Reuters recorded EUR/USD at 1.14755 on 17 September after a 0.7% one-day fall; Commerzbank then revised its path to roughly 1.15 through year-end. Bank of America’s 8 September report, documented subsequently, had already been at 1.15 for year-end versus a Bloomberg median of 1.17. Thus spot moved from about 1.162 at the start toward the lower edge of the public forecast distribution by the close, while medium-term euro recovery views survived mainly at longer horizons.

Source anchors: Reuters, 17 Sep 2026; Commerzbank, 18 Sep 2026; Bank of America report dated 8 Sep 2026 (later public reporting explicitly identifies the report date and 1.15 year-end target).

**Public-bank Q4 / year-end range:** approximately **1.15–1.18** across the visible September sample; the contemporaneous Bloomberg median cited with the Bank of America 8 September report was **1.17**.

**Constructive EUR cluster:** **1.18 Q4 / 1.19–1.20 at 12M**, represented by MUFG, ING’s longer horizon and BNP Paribas’ 12-month view.

**More cautious / tactical view:** **1.15–1.16**, with ING bearish one month and at 1.15 for 1M, Bank of America at 1.15 year-end, and Commerzbank moving to roughly 1.15 through year-end after the Fed meeting.

**Bias at window close:** **near-term neutral-to-bearish EUR / stronger-USD tactical skew; medium-term EUR recovery still present but lower-conviction and more horizon-dependent.**

### What changed through the data window

At the opening of the window, the principal split was between a structural dollar-bearish camp and a tactical dollar-supportive camp. EUR/USD near 1.162 was already close to several three-month/year-end targets, reducing upside asymmetry even before the major central-bank events. ING explicitly downgraded its year-end EUR/USD forecast on 7 September because it expected a Fed hike, while MUFG still expected euro-area resilience and ECB willingness to tighten to support EUR/USD beyond Q3.

The ECB’s 10 September hike did not generate a durable clean euro breakout because it was associated with an adverse energy shock rather than a pure domestic-demand tightening story. The decisive repricing came from the US side: the Fed hiked on 16 September and signalled further tightening, sending EUR/USD down sharply. By 17–18 September the tactical debate had shifted from whether EUR/USD could extend above the 1.16 area toward whether the 1.1450–1.15 zone could hold; Commerzbank’s revised 1.15 year-end profile captured that shift. Forecasts did not uniformly collapse—the longer-horizon 1.18–1.20 euro-recovery camp remained—but spot had moved toward the cautious cluster rather than the constructive one.

### Main consensus drivers

**Relative Fed/ECB path:** The key short-run driver became the Fed’s return to tightening. The Fed’s September hike and hawkish outlook supported the dollar even as the ECB also tightened; the relevant question became which central bank could sustain a firmer path, not simply which one moved first.

**Energy / terms of trade:** High oil and European gas prices were two-sided for EUR: they raised ECB tightening expectations but also weakened European real income, margins and the external balance. MUFG explicitly flagged gas prices as a euro-area growth risk, while BNP Paribas emphasized the United States’ net-energy-exporter position as part of the dollar’s relative resilience to the oil shock.

**Euro-area resilience / fiscal recovery channel:** Stronger euro-area activity and the ECB’s willingness to respond to inflation supported the constructive EUR case, especially beyond the immediate Fed repricing. MUFG treated relative growth and interest-rate expectations as the primary medium-term EUR drivers.

**Structural USD risk premium:** BNP Paribas maintained a longer-run bearish-dollar thesis around fiscal deficits and policy credibility, explaining why some public-bank targets remained near 1.20 at longer horizons despite short-run dollar strength.

### Where consensus could be wrong

**Consensus too bullish EUR:** If US inflation keeps the Fed in a more persistent hiking cycle while European energy costs continue to damage growth and the external balance, the 1.18–1.20 recovery cluster can remain too high even if the ECB tightens further.

**Consensus too cautious EUR:** If Fed tightening proves shorter-lived than priced, energy prices retreat and euro-area growth remains resilient enough for the ECB to hold a relatively firm rate path, spot near 1.15 would leave meaningful room back toward the constructive 1.18–1.20 medium-term cluster.

**Key falsification:** A sustained divergence in the expected Fed–ECB terminal path combined with the direction of European energy prices: **further Fed repricing higher plus persistent European energy stress would falsify the bullish-euro cluster; fading US tightening plus easing energy stress would strengthen it.**

DATA WINDOW: 30 August 2026 to 5 September 2026
A. EUR WEEK — MACRO SYNTHESIS
The euro-area week resolved into a high-headline / contained-underlying inflation regime layered onto a resilient but exceptionally uneven recovery. Manufacturing reached a multi-year high and the bloc composite held around 52, with Germany providing industrial leadership and Italy/Spain strong services support; however, France remained in broad contraction, construction deteriorated to 43.0, and household/rate-sensitive demand stayed weak. The growth signal therefore improved enough to reduce recession risk without becoming a synchronized demand boom. Inflation deteriorated sharply at headline and producer level through energy, but core HICP fell to 2.4%, services inflation slowed to 3.0% and ex-energy PPI was flat m/m, leaving no clean evidence yet of generalized second-round pass-through.
The validated ECB tape sharpens the policy distinction rather than changing the macro regime. The August flash ratified the near-term September tightening case through 3.3% headline inflation and 14.3% energy, while the fall in core and services inflation strengthened the case that the move could be insurance rather than the start of an extended sequence. With no policy-relevant Governing Council remarks inside the window and blackout beginning around 3 September, the committee entered the meeting with the late-August sourced hike-and-close lean intact but the guidance question unresolved. The decisive forward test is the 2027 projection path and whether energy pressure migrates into wages, services prices and non-energy inflation.
B. EUR MACRO SIGNAL SCOREBOARD
Growth: ~
Supporting evidence:
Bloc manufacturing and composite PMIs remained expansionary, with manufacturing at 52.7 and composite at 52.0, Germany strengthening and Italy/Spain services resilient. But the recovery is highly uneven: France contracted across services/composite and construction, Italy and Spain weakened in manufacturing, and euro-area construction fell to 43.0. Net signal: stabilization/expansion without synchronized broad-based demand acceleration.
Labor: ~
Supporting evidence:
The bloc PMI employment signal improved, including the first private-sector employment increase of 2026 and German services hiring returning positive. Against that, construction employment continued to fall and the supplied archive contains no completed official euro-area unemployment release. The labor signal is therefore improving at the margin but insufficiently broad for a clear positive classification.
Inflation: -
Supporting evidence:
Headline HICP accelerated to 3.3% and euro-area PPI to 5.8% y/y, with energy the dominant driver. The adverse headline shock is material, but persistence indicators softened: core HICP fell to 2.4%, services HICP to 3.0%, ex-energy HICP held at 2.2%, and ex-energy PPI was 0.0% m/m. Inflation concern deteriorated at headline level while generalized pass-through remained unconfirmed.
Financial Conditions: -
Supporting evidence:
The rate-sensitive construction recession deepened to a 43.0 PMI, housing was the weakest construction category, new orders deteriorated and borrowing costs remained a stated constraint in Germany. Severe French construction weakness and continued sector employment losses show that restrictive financing conditions are still biting even as manufacturing and services stabilize.
Policy Constraint: -
Supporting evidence:
The validated ECB tape entered blackout with September tightening strongly supported by the 3.3% headline print and the prior sourced Governing Council lean, but with little appetite in that sourced read to signal much beyond the meeting. Core at 2.4%, services at 3.0%, the stable wage-tracker carry-over and severe cross-country/sector weakness all raise the bar for a Q4 extension. The immediate tightening constraint intensified; the terminal-rate constraint is now explicitly two-sided and projection/pass-through dependent.
C. FULL RELEASE ARCHIVE
MONDAY 31 AUG 2026
GERMANY — CPI / HICP PRELIMINARY (AUG)
Release Date: 31 Aug 2026 | Local Time: 14:00
Importance: ***
1. Reuters Data
CPI Prelim MM: 0,20% | Prior: 0,80% | Poll: 0,25% | Surprise: -0,050%
CPI Prelim YY: 2,90% | Prior: 2,80% | Poll: 2,95% | Surprise: -0,050%
HICP Prelim MM: 0,20% | Prior: 0,90% | Poll: 0,30% | Surprise: -0,100%
HICP Prelim YY: 2,90% | Prior: 2,80% | Poll: 3,10% | Surprise: -0,200%
2. Professional Market Commentary
The preliminary release showed German inflation rising further, but less than markets had expected and with the acceleration concentrated in energy.
Destatis reported CPI inflation at 2.9% y/y, with energy inflation accelerating to 10.5% from 8.3%. At the same time, CPI core inflation excluding food and energy remained at 2.4%, services inflation slowed to 2.8% from 2.9%, and food inflation fell to just 0.1%.
The Bundesbank's harmonised-index reading gave the same directional message: energy and non-energy industrial-goods inflation increased, while food and services inflation declined markedly. Its HICP core measure remained at 2.6%.
The release therefore reinforced rather than challenged the emerging euro-area configuration: the external energy shock is lifting headline inflation, but there is still limited evidence of generalized downstream consumer-price acceleration.
3. Comment — Economist Layer
The important signal is not the 0.1pp rise in German headline inflation; it is the increasingly sharp divergence underneath it.
Destatis CPI composition:
- headline: 2.9% vs 2.8%
- energy: 10.5% vs 8.3%
- goods: 3.0% vs 2.5%
- services: 2.8% vs 2.9%
- core excluding food and energy: 2.4%, unchanged
- food: 0.1% vs 0.4%.
The weighting reinforces the interpretation. Services represent just over half of the CPI basket and continued to decelerate, while energy carries a weight of only about 7.4%. Goods inflation moved above services, but this partly reflects the large energy acceleration inside the goods bucket rather than a generalized demand-driven goods-price shock.
All four Reuters inflation rows also undershot consensus. The most relevant miss is HICP y/y at 2.9% versus a 3.1% poll. Germany therefore failed to converge toward the subsequently reported 3.3% euro-area aggregate despite being one of its largest component economies.
There is an important measurement distinction in the core numbers:
- Destatis national CPI excluding food and energy: 2.4%
- Bundesbank HICP excluding energy and food: 2.6%.
These refer to different indices with different coverage and weighting. For comparison with euro-area HICP core, the harmonised measure is conceptually closer; for analysis of the national CPI release, the Destatis 2.4% measure remains the appropriate figure.
The broader pipeline tension remains unresolved. Prior German import-price data showed inflation at 6.8% y/y and materially stronger non-energy pressure, while July PPI had reaccelerated. Consumer prices now show that this upstream pressure has still not translated cleanly into the largest sticky CPI components.
State transition: continuation — headline inflation deteriorates further through energy, while domestic underlying inflation remains broadly stable to softer.
Context from prior regional live file:
German inflation had already shifted into an imported-cost configuration: energy and upstream producer/import prices were accelerating while consumer-level pass-through remained incomplete. August CPI preserves that structure, with the energy shock intensifying but services inflation continuing to ease and national core holding at 2.4%. Germany therefore remains an important test of whether upstream cost pressure eventually propagates into domestic prices rather than evidence that such propagation has already occurred.
4. HF Take — Strategist Layer
The print is less hawkish than the headline acceleration alone suggests.
For the September ECB meeting:
- 2.9% German HICP still confirms that the energy shock is keeping inflation materially above target
- stronger German activity data elsewhere in the tape reduce the growth cost of another hike
- the release therefore does little to challenge a September tightening move.
For the terminal-rate question, however, the composition cuts the other way:
- HICP undershot consensus
- national core did not accelerate
- services inflation fell again
- food inflation is negligible.
The German print therefore strengthens the distinction between an insurance response to the external price shock and a genuine demand-driven tightening cycle.
The next verification test is pass-through. Continued increases in non-energy consumer goods, services or harmonised core inflation would validate the upstream warning from import and producer prices. Continued services/core stability despite elevated energy costs would instead strengthen the case that the shock remains largely relative-price rather than generalized inflation.
Macro configuration:
stronger German growth signal  
- large imported energy shock
- elevated upstream costs
- contained consumer-level core/services inflation
  = supportive of September tightening, but not independently supportive of an extended hiking sequence.
TUESDAY 1 SEP 2026
GERMANY — RETAIL SALES (JUL)
Release Date: 1 Sep 2026 | Local Time: 08:00
Importance: ***
1. Reuters Data
Retail Sales MM Real: -3,4% | Prior: -0,7% | Revised: 0,0% | Poll: 0,4% | Surprise: -3,80%
Retail Sales YY Real: -2,5% | Prior: 0,0% | Revised: 0,6% | Poll: 0,6% | Surprise: -3,10%
2. Professional Market Commentary
Destatis reported a very large fall in real retail turnover, but explicitly identified the expiry of the May-June fuel discount as an important distortion to the headline.
Real sales fell 3.4% m/m while nominal turnover declined only 1.7%. On the year, real turnover fell 2.5% even though nominal sales rose 0.3%. Petrol-station turnover was the clearest source of this wedge: real sales fell 9.1% m/m and 9.3% y/y, while nominal turnover declined only 1.9% m/m and rose 6.9% y/y.
The weakness was not confined to fuel, however. Non-food sales fell 4.8% m/m in real terms and internet/mail-order sales declined 5.6%, providing a cleaner discretionary-demand warning beneath the distorted aggregate.
No Tier 1 institutional debate detected.
3. Comment — Economist Layer
The -3.4% headline substantially overstates the underlying collapse in household demand, but the release is still materially weak after stripping out the obvious fuel distortion.
The first distinction is real versus nominal turnover:
- total retail: -3.4% m/m real vs -1.7% nominal
- total retail: -2.5% y/y real vs +0.3% nominal
- petrol stations: -9.1% m/m real vs -1.9% nominal
- petrol stations: -9.3% y/y real vs +6.9% nominal.
The large real-nominal wedge at petrol stations reflects the reversal of the temporary fuel subsidy. Lower pump prices had mechanically supported real-volume indices during May-June; its expiry raises the deflator and depresses measured real turnover in July.
That explanation cannot account for the entire release.
Sector hierarchy:
- food retail: -0.8% m/m real; -0.3% y/y
- non-food retail: -4.8% m/m real; -3.4% y/y
- internet/mail order: -5.6% m/m real; -0.8% y/y.
Non-food is the key signal because it excludes the petrol-station distortion. Online retail is cleaner still: real turnover fell 5.6% while nominal turnover fell 5.8%, leaving essentially no deflator wedge to explain away the decline.
The June revisions partly soften the sequential message. The prior monthly real reading was revised from -0.7% to 0.0%, while the annual rate was revised from 0.0% to +0.6%.
There is also a material statistical caveat. Destatis comprehensively redesigned the retail short-term statistics beginning with May 2026, including a 2021 base year, Laspeyres indices and a change in reporting units. July is therefore only the third observation under the redesigned system.
The macro implication nonetheless survives that caveat. Germany's recovery remains bifurcated:
corporate / industrial activity ↑
exports / capital expenditure ↑
business expectations ↑
versus
household consumption ~
discretionary retail ↓
purchase intentions weak.
State transition: deterioration — the headline fall is exaggerated by the fuel-subsidy reversal, but non-food and online sales provide genuine hard-data evidence that the household-demand recovery has weakened.
Context from prior regional live file:
The prior tape had already classified Germany's recovery as industrial/export-led rather than household-led: Q2 household consumption rose only marginally and consumer surveys showed persistently weak purchase intentions despite improving economic expectations. July retail sales now provide hard-data confirmation that the household channel has not joined the broader recovery, particularly in discretionary categories. Germany therefore remains a two-speed recovery rather than a generalized domestic-demand expansion.
4. HF Take — Strategist Layer
The release is growth-dovish, but much less dramatically so than the -3.8pp headline surprise suggests.
For the ECB reaction function:
- the petrol-station distortion means the aggregate print should not be interpreted as a sudden collapse in German consumption
- nevertheless, non-food and online weakness confirms that domestic demand remains fragile
- this reduces the quality of the German recovery even as manufacturing improves.
It does not materially challenge a September hike because inflation and energy remain the immediate policy constraint and German recession risk has already fallen.
But it argues against extrapolating stronger German PMIs into a broad overheating story.
For rates, the print is modestly supportive of the dovish side of the post-September debate: stronger industry alongside weak household demand is consistent with a hike-and-close configuration if underlying inflation remains contained.
GERMANY — S&P GLOBAL MANUFACTURING PMI (AUG)
Release Date: 1 Sep 2026 | Local Time: 09:55
Importance: ****
1. Reuters Data
S&P Manufacturing PMI: 54,3 | Prior: 54,1 | Poll: 54,1 | Surprise: 0,20
2. Professional Market Commentary
Germany remained the clear manufacturing leader among the large euro-area economies.
The final PMI was revised up to 54.3 from the 54.1 flash and stood at its strongest level in more than four years. The wider euro-area release highlighted particularly strong export-order growth in Germany, Austria and the Netherlands.
3. Comment — Economist Layer
The final revision validates the survey signal but does not resolve the hard-data contradiction established elsewhere in this week's German tape.
Survey evidence:
- manufacturing PMI 54.3
- strongest level in more than four years
- strong output signal
- strong export-order signal.
But July official data show:
- total orders +2.5%, almost entirely because of large transport-equipment orders
- orders excluding large orders -1.4%
- three-month ex-large orders -2.2%
- non-euro-area orders -10.1%
- real manufacturing turnover -1.5% m/m.
Part of the contradiction may be timing: PMI responses collected in August can lead July hard statistics. Part may also be definition: PMI export orders include intra-euro-area orders, while official data showed euro-area demand surging and extra-euro-area demand falling.
Germany can therefore report improving PMI "exports" while much of the impulse actually reflects intra-European procurement and defence/infrastructure flows rather than a broad revival of global demand.
State transition: continuation — the German manufacturing survey acceleration is confirmed and marginally strengthened, but breadth and hard-data transmission remain unresolved.
Context from prior regional live file:
The August flash had already established Germany's clearest industrial-recovery signal in years. The final strengthens that survey evidence, but subsequent hard data show the improvement remains concentrated in large orders, fiscal/defence-linked sectors and intra-European demand. Germany remains the principal industrial recovery node, but its transition from survey recovery to broad realized manufacturing expansion is not yet complete.
4. HF Take — Strategist Layer
Meaningfully supportive of the ECB's near-term growth cover, but not sufficient evidence for a prolonged tightening cycle.
September implications:
- recession risk is lower
- German manufacturing confidence is strong
- the ECB can respond to the energy shock without tightening into an obvious German industrial contraction.
Post-September, the question is whether the improvement broadens beyond defence/transport equipment, intra-European demand and survey expectations.
This PMI provides growth-cover hawkishness, not yet overheating hawkishness.

Istat framed the August acceleration as predominantly an energy-price event rather than a broadening domestic inflation shock.
National CPI rose to 3.3% y/y from 2.9%, while energy inflation accelerated sharply to 17.0% from 11.6%. Both non-regulated energy prices rose to 16.9% from 11.4% and regulated energy to 18.8% from 14.8%.
The underlying picture moved in the opposite direction. Core inflation eased to 1.5% from 1.6%, inflation excluding energy slowed to 1.7% from 1.8%, and services inflation declined to 2.4% from 2.7%.
The harmonised HICP rose only 0.1% m/m because summer sales are captured in HICP but not in the national NIC index.
3. Comment — Economist Layer
The headline reversal is large, but the composition remains unusually benign outside energy.
Key hierarchy:
- total energy: 17.0% from 11.6%
- non-regulated energy: 16.9% from 11.4%
- regulated energy: 18.8% from 14.8%
- goods: 4.1% from 3.2%
- services: 2.4% from 2.7%
- core excluding energy and fresh food: 1.5% from 1.6%
- excluding energy: 1.7% from 1.8%.
The key change versus July is inside energy. In July, non-regulated energy had been decelerating while regulated prices were catching up. In August, both components accelerate simultaneously.
But that deterioration has not propagated into the sticky domestic basket.
There is nevertheless a household-perception channel worth preserving. Prices of frequently purchased products accelerated to 4.3% from 3.4%, even though the broader household shopping basket remained around 1%.
The acquired inflation split reinforces the distinction:
- 2026 headline carry: 2.9%
- 2026 core carry: 1.9%.
State transition: reversal — July's headline stabilization reverses sharply through energy, while the underlying domestic inflation trend continues to soften.
Context from prior regional live file:
July had marked a stabilization in Italian inflation, with headline rates easing, core inflation at 1.6% and non-regulated energy pressure moderating even as regulated energy accelerated. August reverses the headline improvement because both energy channels now rise together, but core and services soften further. Italy therefore remains a clear example of an external headline shock without synchronized second-round domestic inflation.
4. HF Take — Strategist Layer
The release is hawkish for the September ECB decision through the headline and energy channel, but distinctly less hawkish for the terminal-rate debate.
Near-term:
- headline inflation has reaccelerated materially
- both administered and market energy channels are now pushing higher.
But the persistence test remains negative:
- HICP undershot consensus by 0.2pp
- core fell to 1.5%
- services fell to 2.4%
- ex-energy inflation slowed.
Italy therefore strengthens the case for an ECB insurance response to an externally generated inflation shock, but not the case that domestic demand or wage/service persistence requires a prolonged hiking cycle.

2. Professional Market Commentary
Euro-area manufacturing recorded its strongest expansion in more than four years.
The final PMI reached 52.7, up from July's 51.9 but 0.1 below the flash estimate. The output index increased to 53.3, its highest level in 54 months. New orders rose at the fastest pace since early 2022, export business expanded for only the second time in four and a half years, and manufacturing employment stabilized after more than three years of continuous decline.

3. Comment — Economist Layer
The August final is genuinely strong at the bloc level, but the quality of that strength is more complicated than the 52.7 headline suggests.
Positive signals:
- PMI at a 51-month high
- output at a 54-month high
- strongest new-order growth since early 2022
- export orders growing
- employment no longer contracting
- confidence improving.

First, country dispersion has widened sharply:
Germany: 54.3
France: 51.1
Italy: 49.6
Spain: 49.5.
Second, supplier delivery times lengthened markedly. Because slower delivery times contribute positively to the manufacturing PMI, some headline strength reflects supply constraint rather than demand.
Third, the German hard-data contradiction remains unresolved. The bloc's strong export-order narrative can coexist with falling German non-euro-area orders because PMI export measures include intra-euro-area trade.
The emerging hypothesis is therefore:
European fiscal / defence / capital-goods demand  
- intra-European procurement
- improving manufacturing sentiment
rather than
uniform global final-demand acceleration.
State transition: improvement — euro-area manufacturing expansion broadens into orders, exports and employment stabilization, but the recovery remains geographically uneven and partly supply/fiscal-driven rather than a clean generalized demand boom.
Context from prior regional live file:

The final barely revises that signal, but the completed country set reveals materially greater dispersion: Italy and Spain are now contracting while Germany strengthens. The regional industrial recovery remains valid, but its centre of gravity has shifted decisively toward Germany and intra-European/capital-goods demand.
4. HF Take — Strategist Layer
The manufacturing final strengthens the ECB's growth cover for the September hike.
It shows:
- no bloc-wide industrial recession
- strengthening forward orders
- some recovery in exports
- an end to persistent manufacturing job shedding
- moderating producer-price inflation despite the energy shock.
But it does not independently justify an extended hiking sequence because manufacturing inflation is easing, Italy and Spain have moved into contraction, German hard data remain less impressive than the survey, and services/core consumer inflation remain more important for persistence.
For rates: September supported; additional tightening needs downstream inflation validation.

The flash confirmed a further sharp rise in headline inflation but with a distinctly softer underlying composition.

By contrast, services inflation slowed to 3.0% from 3.3%, core inflation eased to 2.4% from 2.5%, and inflation excluding energy remained at 2.2%.

The professional policy debate therefore remained split between a near-term ECB response to the persistent energy shock and caution over extrapolating a sustained hiking cycle.
3. Comment — Economist Layer
The key signal is the widening divergence between headline inflation and domestic underlying inflation.
Headline HICP reached 3.3%, above the May peak of 3.2% and therefore the highest level of the current energy-shock phase.

- food, alcohol & tobacco: 1.2%, unchanged.

- HICP excluding energy: 2.2%, unchanged for a third month
- excluding energy and unprocessed food: 2.1%, down from 2.2%
- core excluding energy, food, alcohol & tobacco: 2.4%, down from 2.5%
- all exclusion aggregates: +0.2% m/m versus +0.4% for headline.
This means the August headline acceleration does not yet represent generalized consumer-price broadening. Services — the largest and more domestically persistent bucket — actually decelerated.
The cross-country distribution also remains unusually wide. Spain stood materially above Germany and France, showing that the aggregate shock is not a uniform large-economy domestic inflation process.
State transition: continuation — the external energy inflation shock intensifies materially, while underlying consumer inflation remains contained and services momentum actually softens.
Context from prior regional live file:

August intensifies the headline shock but strengthens rather than weakens the evidence of a split between energy inflation and domestic persistence. The unresolved regional regime therefore remains upstream/headline inflation pressure without confirmed generalized downstream pass-through.
4. HF Take — Strategist Layer
The print strengthens the case for the September ECB hike without providing equally strong evidence for an extended tightening cycle.
Near-term reaction function:
- headline inflation at 3.3% and the renewed energy shock make inaction increasingly difficult
- improving regional growth gives the ECB more room to deliver another insurance hike.
Post-September reaction function is materially less clear:
- core inflation fell
- services inflation slowed
- ex-energy inflation remains stable
- no convincing consumer-level second-round broadening is yet visible.
The decisive next test is transmission rather than the headline energy rate itself: services inflation, wages, firms' selling prices and non-energy consumer inflation must begin to accelerate if the shock is to justify a persistent tightening cycle.
Macro configuration:
growth recovery / resilience  
- severe external energy shock
- contained underlying consumer inflation
  = September tightening strongly supported, terminal-rate extension still conditional.

2. Professional Market Commentary
Italian producer-price inflation accelerated sharply in July, but Istat explicitly attributed the move primarily to the domestic energy component.

producer energy pressure ↑↑
headline CPI ↑↑
core CPI ↓
services CPI ↓.

D. CENTRAL BANK TAPE
Summary — Policy reaction function
The window was speaker-empty but policy-dense. No Governing Council member delivered policy-relevant remarks between 30 August and the blackout, so the decisive in-window input was the 1 September inflation flash: headline HICP rose to 3.3% and energy to 14.3%, while core fell to 2.4% and services to 3.0%. In the validated tape, that combination ratified the September hike while simultaneously strengthening the case for hike-and-close rather than an automatic Q4 sequence. Carry-over Governing Council sourcing still pointed to a September hike with little appetite to signal beyond, while the final pre-blackout named voices had been hawkish. The forward reaction-function hinge is therefore no longer whether headline inflation warrants the September move, but whether the 2027 projection path and subsequent energy-to-core / wage pass-through justify another one.

2. Could the September projections mark 2027 inflation materially higher despite falling realized core/services, thereby validating continued tightening even if current underlying inflation is soft?

H. CURRENCY MARKET-CONSENSUS SCAN
Bottom line
The point-in-time EUR/USD consensus during 30 August–5 September was mildly constructive on the euro over the medium term but much less clean tactically. A Reuters poll conducted 31 August–2 September showed median EUR/USD forecasts of 1.16 in three months, 1.17 in six months and 1.18 in twelve months, versus spot around the 1.16 area. Strategists broadly expected the dollar to remain firm near term but weaken over a year, with the main disagreement centered on how far Fed tightening would ultimately go.
Conviction weakened through the window rather than reversing outright. ING shifted on 3 September to a stronger-for-longer dollar view after moving its Fed call toward a September hike, cutting its end-2026 EUR/USD target to 1.16 from 1.18. By contrast, UBS on 2 September still expected EUR/USD to move toward 1.18–1.20 over time, arguing that markets would ultimately scale back Fed tightening expectations while the ECB could tighten again. The result was a split between a tactically capped EUR around 1.16 and a still-constructive medium-term EUR view.
Public-bank end-2026 / medium-term range: 1.16–1.20 in the clearly dated contemporaneous public sample.
Constructive EUR cluster: 1.18–1.20.
More cautious / tactical view: around 1.16.
Bias at window close: mildly constructive EUR medium term, but near-term asymmetry was capped by Fed repricing, high U.S. yields and the energy/geopolitical shock.
What changed through the data window
At the start of the window, EUR/USD had retreated toward 1.16 after Kevin Warsh’s hawkish Jackson Hole signal and renewed U.S.-Iran conflict revived Fed-hike and safe-haven support for the dollar. The Reuters poll showed that medium-term dollar-weakness forecasts had barely changed from August, so most of the adjustment was initially spot convergence and tactical repricing rather than wholesale forecast capitulation.
During the window, euro-area inflation reinforced expectations of an ECB hike, but that support was offset by a parallel rise in U.S. tightening expectations and global yields. The important forecast change was ING’s 3 September revision from 1.18 to 1.16 for end-2026; UBS maintained a more constructive 1.18–1.20 path. Consensus therefore became less one-directional: EUR upside remained in the medium-term forecast distribution, but the clean near-term long-EUR trade was increasingly capped.
Main consensus drivers
Fed/ECB policy differential: The dominant tactical driver was the repricing of Fed tightening after Warsh’s hawkish turn. EUR support from expected ECB tightening existed, but the relative policy impulse no longer pointed cleanly in one direction.
U.S. yield / fiscal tension: Higher Treasury yields supported the dollar cyclically, but some investors distinguished between yield driven by tighter policy and yield driven by fiscal/debasement concerns, limiting the durability of dollar support.
Energy / geopolitics: Renewed U.S.-Iran conflict and higher oil increased both European inflation pressure and safe-haven USD demand. For EUR, this created a negative terms-of-trade and risk-premium channel even as it strengthened the case for an ECB hike.
European resilience versus dispersion: Better euro-area aggregate PMIs and the expected ECB move supported the euro, but France/construction weakness and the lack of generalized inflation pass-through limited confidence in a prolonged ECB tightening cycle.
Where consensus could be wrong
Consensus too bullish EUR: If Fed tightening proved more persistent than strategists expected, U.S. yields stayed elevated and the energy shock continued to penalize Europe’s terms of trade, EUR/USD could remain below the 1.18–1.20 constructive cluster for longer.
Consensus too cautious EUR: If U.S. inflation/labor data forced markets to unwind Fed-hike pricing while the ECB still delivered its expected September hike and European growth held up, the dollar could weaken faster and EUR/USD could re-enter the upper end of the public target distribution.
Key falsification: A durable break in the relative policy path — either sustained Fed tightening without a comparable ECB extension, or a clear Fed repricing lower while euro-area activity remains resilient — would invalidate the balanced 1.16-near-term / 1.18–1.20-medium-term consensus structure.
Sources: Reuters FX poll, 2 Sep 2026; ING THINK, 3 Sep 2026; UBS CIO, 2 Sep 2026.

DATA WINDOW: 16 August 2026 to 29 August 2026

A. EUR WEEK — MACRO SYNTHESIS

The euro-area regime shifted further toward **growth recovery with an externally driven inflation shock rather than generalized domestic overheating**. Germany moved decisively from survey-led stabilization into a validated industrial/export recovery: GDP, PMIs, ZEW and Ifo all strengthened, while bloc-wide PMIs showed improving orders, exports and employment. France moved in the opposite direction, with Q2 growth revised to zero, services activity contracting and labour conditions softening; Spain remained the stronger-growth/high-inflation pole. Across the region, the corporate/external cycle recovered considerably faster than household demand, investment or hard employment.

Inflation became the principal policy constraint. Headline inflation and upstream import/producer costs deteriorated materially, including clear non-energy broadening in German imports and French PPI, but consumer-level transmission remained incomplete: French services inflation fell, Spanish core softened and euro-area PMI selling-price pressure moderated. The validated ECB tape converts this macro configuration into a much firmer near-term policy signal: **a September 25bp hike is now near-locked, while the post-September path remains explicitly contested.** The sourced committee lean points toward **hike-and-close**, whereas Schnabel's “insufficient” framing preserves a further-tightening wing. The regime is therefore **growth stabilization/acceleration + headline/upstream inflation pressure + near-term ECB tightening + unresolved downstream pass-through**, with the key policy question shifting from whether September happens to whether the cost shock justifies continuation into Q4.

B. EUR MACRO SIGNAL SCOREBOARD

Growth: +

Supporting evidence:
Euro-area composite PMI reached 52.1 with stronger new orders, exports and employment; EC economic sentiment recovered to 98.4; Germany recorded a third consecutive positive GDP quarter and a marked manufacturing/Ifo/ZEW acceleration. France remained a material drag after Q2 GDP was revised to 0.0%, preventing the signal from becoming a generalized domestic-demand boom, but the regional growth distribution improved clearly over the window.

Labor: ~

Supporting evidence:
Survey flows improved: euro-area PMI employment increased for the first time in 2026, EC employment expectations rose to 98.9 and German unemployment deterioration slowed. Hard stocks remain weaker: German employment was still -226k y/y, French registered jobseekers increased and French services employment remained soft. Labour therefore looks like a lagging stabilization rather than a confirmed expansion.

Inflation: -

Supporting evidence:
Headline and upstream inflation pressure worsened: euro-area HICP remained 2.9%, French HICP rose to 2.7%, Spanish HICP to 4.5%, German import prices reached +6.8% y/y and non-energy imported inflation +4.8%, while French ex-energy PPI rose to 2.7%. The deterioration is mitigated by softer French services inflation, lower Spanish core and weaker PMI selling-price pressure, but inflation risk clearly increased at the pipeline/headline level.

Financial Conditions: +

Supporting evidence:
M3 growth held at 3.4%, adjusted private-sector lending accelerated to 4.1% and NFC lending to 4.4%. Corporate deposits also strengthened. Monetary transmission remains active through deposit substitution, but financing availability does not resemble a broad credit crunch and is not yet preventing the corporate recovery.

Policy Constraint: -

Supporting evidence:
The policy constraint hardened materially over the window. Stronger regional growth, lower German recession risk, headline inflation overshoots and broad upstream cost pressure were followed by a sourced Governing Council lean toward a September hike, Schnabel arguing that current policy remains “insufficient” to return inflation sustainably to target and Dolenc describing a September move as having a “strong case.” September is therefore near-locked. The remaining constraint is asymmetric: the sourced committee shows little appetite to pre-commit beyond September, while the hawkish wing and market pricing preserve a meaningful Q4 continuation risk.

D. CENTRAL BANK TAPE

Summary — Policy reaction function

The ECB communication regime crystallized materially during the final pre-blackout fortnight. A September 25bp hike moved from a strongly live scenario to a **near-decided policy action**, supported by stronger growth, persistent headline inflation and a sourced Governing Council lean. The key disagreement is no longer September direction but **what comes after it**: Reuters' sourced committee read points toward a hike-and-close strategy with little appetite to signal further tightening, while Schnabel's stronger “insufficient” framing preserves a second-hike argument. Market pricing at window close was therefore somewhat more hawkish than the sourced intended guidance, making the September communication asymmetry potentially dovish even if the rate decision itself is hawkish.

Governing Council sourced lean — ~25 August 2026
Importance: ****

Key policy signal:
Reuters reporting based on three sources indicated that policymakers were leaning toward a September hike to contain the inflationary impact of the war, but showed little appetite to signal a further tightening sequence beyond that move.

Representative quote:
“little appetite to signal further tightening beyond that”

Incremental reaction function:
This substantially resolves the September decision while simultaneously capping the inferred forward path. The committee's central configuration becomes **hike-and-close** rather than an automatic hiking cycle. Confidence is Medium-High because the signal is sourced reporting rather than an official statement; Dolenc corroborates the direction, but not the “little beyond” guidance component.

Schnabel — late August 2026
Importance: ***

Key policy signal:
Schnabel re-entered the policy debate arguing that current policy remained insufficient to return inflation sustainably to the 2% target, while stronger growth and improved sentiment reduced the force of the activity objection.

Representative quote:
“insufficient”

Incremental reaction function:
This is a stronger hawkish rung than simply arguing that rates may need to rise further. It establishes the internal case for continuation beyond September if projections or subsequent inflation data show persistent second-round pressure. The precise venue/date remains unpinned in the supplied tape, so confidence is capped at Medium-High.

Dolenc — 28 August 2026
Importance: ***

Key policy signal:
At Jackson Hole, Dolenc argued that September had a strong case because inflation risks remained elevated, growth had exceeded expectations and the geopolitical/energy shock had not materially improved.

Representative quote:
“strong case”

Incremental reaction function:
Provides on-record corroboration that the September move is not merely sourced committee speculation. Stronger growth has effectively removed the near-term activity veto; energy/inflation risk is now the dominant decision input.

ECB — Accounts of the 22–23 July meeting — in-window release
Importance: **

Key policy signal:
The July accounts described the contemporaneous backdrop as broadly consistent with holding rates steady.

Representative quote:
“broadly consistent” with holding.

Incremental reaction function:
The document mainly illustrates the speed of the state transition. A hold-consistent July snapshot had been overtaken by the August combination of firmer activity, persistent headline inflation and hawkish communication before the September meeting.

Bottom line — central bank tape

**September 25bp is near-locked.** The reaction-function debate has moved one meeting forward. The sourced majority appears to favour **hike-and-close**, whereas Schnabel represents the case for keeping an explicit tightening bias alive. The decisive Q4 variables are no longer whether growth can tolerate one hike, but whether upstream energy/import pressure reaches wages/services/core inflation and whether the September projections validate persistence. The main communication risk is therefore a **hawkish decision with a comparatively dovish market reaction** if the ECB delivers the hike while deliberately closing forward guidance.

E. SIGNAL TENSION CHECK

Main contradiction:
The September decision is increasingly resolved hawkishly even though the underlying inflation evidence remains much less decisive than the headline/upstream shock. Policy is moving toward another hike while French services inflation, Spanish core and euro-area selling-price indicators do not yet show generalized second-round acceleration.

Why it matters:
This distinction determines whether September is the endpoint of a pre-emptive energy/import response or the beginning of a renewed tightening sequence.

Implication:
The main post-September test is whether elevated imported/producer costs transmit into wages, services and core inflation. Failure to do so favours the sourced **hike-and-close** majority; visible second-round pass-through strengthens Schnabel's continuation case.

F. 5 KEY RELEASES TO DIG INTO

**** EURO ZONE FLASH PMIs (21 AUG)
Why it matters: The strongest regional growth signal of the window: composite 52.1, stronger manufacturing, new orders, exports and employment, but softer selling-price pressure. It simultaneously removed much of the near-term growth objection to tightening and exposed the inventory/supply/final-demand composition question.

**** GERMANY FLASH PMIs (21 AUG)
Why it matters: Manufacturing at 54.1 provided the cleanest early validation that the German industrial recovery was real rather than survey optimism. The unresolved issue is whether an export/manufacturing rebound can broaden while services remain below 50.

**** FRANCE GDP FINAL Q2 (28 AUG)
Why it matters: The preliminary +0.2% rebound disappeared, materially widening the France/Germany divergence. The zero headline is inventory-distorted, but weak investment, purchasing power and labour input leave France as the large-country growth laggard.

**** GERMANY IFO (25 AUG)
Why it matters: Broad beats in current conditions and expectations confirmed the German cycle turn across surveys and sectors. The remaining transmission test is whether production/confidence feed into orders, capex, employment and households.

**** FRANCE CPI/HICP FLASH (28 AUG)
Why it matters: Headline HICP rose to 2.7%, but services inflation fell back to 2.0%. This directly weakened the July broadening hypothesis and sharpened the distinction between energy-driven headline inflation and domestic persistence.

G. RED TEAM QUESTIONS

1. Is the August euro-area manufacturing acceleration sustainable once precautionary stockbuilding, supply delays and temporary defence/technology demand normalize?

2. Can Germany convert an export/manufacturing recovery into private investment, employment and household spending before external demand or inventories weaken?

3. Do German ex-energy import inflation at 4.8% and French ex-energy PPI at 2.7% eventually transmit into wages/services/core inflation, or predominantly into margins and weaker capex?

4. Does the next euro-area inflation round preserve the energy-headline / contained-underlying split, or finally show generalized services/core acceleration?

5. Is the sourced **hike-and-close** committee read correct, or does September communication retain an explicit further-tightening bias closer to Schnabel's “insufficient” framing?

6. With a September hike near-locked but further Q4 tightening heavily priced, is the larger market risk now a dovish repricing after a hawkish decision if Lagarde deliberately closes forward guidance?

7. Do subsequent hard labour data validate improving PMI/EC employment intentions, or confirm that the regional recovery remains unusually productivity/external-demand intensive?

H. CURRENCY MARKET-CONSENSUS SCAN

### Bottom line

Pair convention: EUR/USD.

The publicly visible institutional bias entering the window was **modestly constructive EUR over the medium term but much less uniform tactically**. The August forecast set placed the central public cluster in the mid/high-1.10s, with a more constructive upper tail around 1.20–1.21. The directional argument rested on a combination of dollar weakness, European policy resilience and an improving euro-area growth picture, but conviction was materially lower at tactical horizons.

The window produced more **spot convergence and tactical re-pricing than broad formal forecast revision**. EUR/USD started the first trading day around 1.1578 as softer U.S. data reduced Fed-tightening expectations. European data subsequently became more supportive, but by the second week the pair had already traded into the cautious/public-consensus zone, reducing the asymmetry of chasing the medium-term constructive view.

By 25 August, a cautious institutional reading placed EUR/USD fair value around 1.16 even as spot traded near 1.167, arguing that part of the euro's strength reflected a USD/Treasury risk premium rather than European fundamentals alone. The pair then closed 28 August around 1.1598 after the hawkish Jackson Hole repricing of the dollar. The key point is therefore that the medium-term EUR view remained constructive, while late-window tactical asymmetry was significantly less attractive.

**Public-bank Q4 2026 range:** **1.16–1.21**

**Constructive EUR cluster:** **1.18–1.21**

**More cautious / tactical view:** **~1.16**

**Bias at window close:** **medium-term constructive EUR, tactically much less compelling around 1.16**. Spot had already reached the cautious/public-consensus zone and briefly traded above it, while the more bullish 1.18–1.21 forecasts still required further dollar weakness and/or stronger European catalysts.

### What changed through the data window

At the start of the window, the immediate EUR/USD move was principally a **Fed/USD story**. Softer U.S. labour, retail and inflation information reduced September Fed-hike expectations and squeezed a large long-dollar position.

European fundamentals then became more supportive. Stronger euro-area activity and inflation information reinforced expectations of another ECB move and provided a genuine local EUR catalyst rather than leaving the pair solely dependent on dollar weakness.

By the latter part of the window, valuation asymmetry became more evident. EUR/USD had already moved toward the existing medium-term forecast distribution, while some institutional models still placed rate/fundamental fair value closer to the 1.16 area or below. The Jackson Hole reversal then demonstrated how dependent the pair remained on the U.S. rates leg.

There is **no strong public evidence of a wholesale forecast-target reset during 16–29 August**. The cleaner change was tactical: spot moved toward existing targets, USD sentiment deteriorated and then partially reversed, and the European macro leg became more supportive. Forecast change and spot convergence should therefore not be conflated.

### Main consensus drivers

**Relative policy / rates:**
The euro gained support as stronger European activity and inflation made another ECB hike increasingly credible while weak U.S. data temporarily reduced Fed-tightening expectations. The late-window hawkish Fed repricing showed that this differential remained highly reversible.

**USD structural / Treasury premium:**
A material part of the EUR/USD upside was attributed to discomfort with U.S. Treasury policy, long-end yields and a broader dollar policy premium rather than Europe alone.

**European growth re-rating:**
The strengthening Germany/euro-area activity picture increasingly provided a genuine local EUR catalyst, reducing the extent to which the constructive EUR call depended exclusively on USD weakness.

**Energy / domestic risk premium:**
Higher energy prices remained a two-sided euro factor: they strengthened the ECB inflation case but threatened European terms of trade, margins and real domestic demand.

### Where consensus could be wrong

**Consensus too bullish EUR:**
A sustained Fed repricing toward further hikes, normalization of the Treasury/dollar credibility premium, continued high U.S. yields or an energy shock that damages European growth faster than it lifts ECB rates could push EUR/USD back below the mid-1.10s.

**Consensus too cautious EUR:**
If dollar diversification persists while the euro-area recovery broadens and the ECB remains tighter than previously expected, EUR/USD could move toward the 1.18–1.21 constructive cluster rather than stopping around the 1.16 public-consensus/fair-value area.

**Key falsification:**
The decisive combination is **Fed/ECB relative repricing + persistence or reversal of the U.S. Treasury/dollar risk premium**. A hawkish Fed combined with normalization of the dollar policy premium would invalidate the constructive EUR asymmetry; continued USD-policy pressure alongside resilient euro-area growth and ECB tightening would strengthen it.

DATA WINDOW: 27 July 2026 to 8 August 2026

# A. EUR WEEK — MACRO SYNTHESIS

The euro-area regime shifted materially from spring fragility toward **confirmed but uneven resilience**. Q2 GDP at +0.4% q/q and July services/composite PMIs at 51.7/52.0 raised the regional growth floor: Spain is in broad domestic expansion, Germany has developed a credible industrial/export recovery with early services stabilization, Italy remains services/domestic-led, while France is still the major-country laggard. But June retail weakness, contracting construction, weak French/Italian industrial data and softer German/French labour breadth prevent a broad demand-overheating classification. Inflation remains **above target, energy-heavy and highly heterogeneous**: Spain combines the strongest domestic growth with the stickiest underlying inflation, France introduces a new services-persistence risk, while Germany and Italy do not confirm the same underlying acceleration.

The central-bank tape materially hardens the policy read. Kazimir explicitly argued for pre-emption before second-round effects become visible, while the two decisive in-window data releases both cut hawkish: Q2 GDP doubled consensus at +0.4% q/q and July HICP reaccelerated to 2.9%, with core at 2.5% and services at 3.3%. With no in-window dovish counter-tape during the summer recess, the reaction function shifts from **September merely live** to **a 25bp September hike as the loaded base case**, while still retaining meaningful conditionality around the GDP revision, August inflation, wages and energy. The likely destination is increasingly one additional insurance hike rather than the beginning of a mechanically extrapolated hiking cycle.

# B. EUR MACRO SIGNAL SCOREBOARD

Growth: +
Supporting evidence:
Q2 euro-area GDP rose 0.4% q/q versus 0.2% expected, materially reducing recession risk. July composite PMI reached 52.0 and services 51.7, with fresh new-order growth; Germany manufacturing strengthened to 52.2, Spain services reached 58.3 and Italy composite rose to 52.5. The improvement remains uneven because France is still below 50, euro-area retail sales fell 0.3% m/m, Germany retail fell 0.7%, Italy IP fell 1.0% and construction remains contracting.

Labor: ~
Supporting evidence:
Euro-area unemployment remains historically low at 6.3%, and Spain continues to generate strong employment alongside rising participation. But labour breadth is weakening: German unemployment rose 6k SA, the rate reached 6.4%, payroll employment is falling and labour demand remains weak; France's broader labour trajectory is also deteriorating. Italy's unemployment rise is mainly participation-driven, so the aggregate has softened without yet breaking.

Inflation: -
Supporting evidence:
July euro-area HICP remained 2.9%, core rose to 2.5% and services to 3.3%. Spain combines HICP at 3.8%, core around 3% and strong domestic demand; France surprised materially higher with services inflation rising from 1.9% to 2.3%. Germany's headline rebound is more energy-driven and Italy's underlying inflation remains comparatively benign, while producer/import-price momentum is stabilizing. Inflation therefore remains an active constraint, but generalized second-round acceleration is still unconfirmed.

Financial Conditions: ~
Supporting evidence:
M3 growth at 3.3%, household loan growth around 3.0% and NFC loan growth around 4.0% show that monetary transmission is no longer deteriorating sharply. Credit has moved away from outright contraction but has not accelerated into a boom, leaving financial conditions closer to neutral than to either renewed restriction or strong cyclical stimulus.

Policy Constraint: -
Supporting evidence:
The macro tape already removed much of the growth objection to another hike through Q2 GDP at +0.4% and stronger July PMIs. The central-bank scout hardens that signal materially: Kazimir argued that at least one more hike is likely needed and explicitly framed policy around acting before second-round effects become visible, while July HICP reaccelerated to 2.9%, core to 2.5% and services to 3.3%. With the conditional/dovish camp silent during the recess, September moves from optionality to the **loaded 25bp base case**, albeit still vulnerable to the 14 August GDP revision, late-August wage data, oil and the 1 September HICP flash.

The administrative series is affected by the 2025 full-employment-law registration change.

A later INSEE ILO cross-check showed Q2 unemployment at 8.3%, up 0.2pp and the sixth consecutive rise.

**3. Comment — Economist Layer**

The correct interpretation is **slow labour deterioration masked by a major administrative break**, not a sudden unemployment surge.

The Reuters monthly increase is small, but the broader ILO trajectory confirms that French labour conditions are weakening.

State transition: **deterioration — earlier improvement has stalled and broader labour indicators are softening.**

**4. HF Take — Strategist Layer**

Mildly dovish for the ECB through French growth quality.

The labour block becomes more important because French inflation subsequently surprises higher despite weakening employment breadth.

### EURO ZONE — HICP FLASH / CORE HICP (JUL)

Importance: ****

**1. Reuters Data**

HICP YY: 2,9% | Prior: 2,8% | Poll: 2,9% | Surprise: 0,00%

Core HICP YY: 2,5% | Prior: 2,4% | Poll: 2,4% | Surprise: +0,10%

Core HICP MM: 0,00% | Prior: +0,20% | Poll: +0,10% | Surprise: -0,10%

**2. Professional Market Commentary**

Components:

* energy: 10.0% y/y from 8.5%;
* services: 3.3% from 3.2%;
* food/alcohol/tobacco: 1.2% from 1.5%;
* non-energy industrial goods: 0.9% from 0.7%.

The market/economist policy split widened: markets were pricing a more extended hiking path, while institutional economists generally remained closer to one additional move.

Pantheon expected one further 25bp increase followed by a pause.

**3. Comment — Economist Layer**

The release is **hawkish in annual terms but much less alarming sequentially**.

The 0.0% core m/m figure is not seasonally adjusted and therefore cannot be treated as a clean underlying-momentum measure.

Inside core:

* services rose sharply m/m due in part to summer travel;
* goods fell sharply due in part to summer sales.

So the correct interpretation is:

* direct energy inflation remains high;
* annual core and services are somewhat firmer;
* no broad net monthly core increase occurred;
* generalized second-round effects remain unconfirmed.

State transition: **continuation — above-target energy inflation persists with modest underlying firmness, but no confirmed broad second-round acceleration.**

**4. HF Take — Strategist Layer**

This keeps September **live**, but does not settle it.

Hawkish case:

* GDP +0.4%;
* HICP 2.9%;
* core 2.5%;
* services 3.3%.

Hold case:

* underlying monthly net momentum limited;
* labour softening;
* national dispersion very wide;
* much of the headline pressure remains energy-driven.

Reaction function: **growth resilience removes the recession constraint; persistence of services/wages determines whether another hike is necessary rather than merely optional.**
